title: Facilitate learning using a variety of given methodologies

lessons.title: The facilitator's role and adult learning
lessons.html:
From trainer to facilitator

Agricultural extension officers, Landcare facilitators and farm trainers work mostly with adults: farm workers, smallholder farmers, community members and supervisors. A facilitator does not just "tell". A facilitator creates conditions in which people learn by doing, discussing and reflecting, and draws on what they already know. In South Africa's outcomes-based system, learning is judged by what the learner can demonstrate, so facilitation must link to the specific outcomes and assessment criteria of the unit standard or programme.

Principles of adult learning

  • Relevance – adults learn when they see how it solves a real problem on their farm or project.
  • Experience – they bring years of practical knowledge. Use it; do not ignore it.
  • Self-direction – involve them in setting goals and choosing activities.
  • Respect – avoid talking down; respect culture, age and language.
  • Practice and feedback – learning sticks when people try, get feedback and try again.

The experiential learning cycle

Kolb's cycle is a useful frame: concrete experience (do something, e.g. a field visit to an eroded donga) → reflection (what did we see?) → conceptualisation (why does it happen? what principles apply?) → active experimentation (plan and build a stone pack, then observe it after the next rain). A good session moves learners around the whole cycle.

Know your learners

Before facilitating, find out learners' literacy and numeracy levels, home languages, prior knowledge, physical needs, and the context they work in. A group of commercial farm supervisors in the Western Cape needs a different approach from a rural village garden group in Limpopo. Plan for language: use interpreters or co-facilitators, visual materials and local examples. Consider recognition of prior learning (RPL) where learners already have competence.

lessons.title: Choosing and using methodologies
lessons.html:
A toolbox of methods

MethodBest forWatch out for
Short input / mini-lectureNew facts, concepts, legal requirementsKeep it under 15–20 minutes; use visuals
DemonstrationSkills: grafting, calibrating a sprayer, building a contourEveryone must see; follow with practice
Guided practiceBuilding competenceEnough materials; safety supervision
Group discussion / buzz groupsSharing experience, problem solvingDominant voices; give roles
Case studyApplying principles to real situationsMake it local and realistic
Role playConflict, negotiation, extension conversationsDebrief carefully; respect comfort levels
Field visit / farmer field schoolObservation, peer learningLogistics, transport, permission
Participatory tools (mapping, transect walk, seasonal calendar)Community analysis and planningNeeds skilled facilitation

Choosing well

Match the method to the outcome: knowledge outcomes suit inputs and reading; skill outcomes need demonstration and practice; attitude and behaviour outcomes need discussion, reflection and role play. Consider group size, time, venue (often outdoors with no electricity), resources and learner profile. Mixing methods keeps energy up and caters for different learning preferences.

Demonstration technique (tell–show–do–review)

  1. Explain the purpose and safety points.
  2. Demonstrate at normal speed, then slowly with explanation.
  3. Learners practise while you observe and coach.
  4. Review: what went well, what to improve.

lessons.title: Running the session and reviewing it
lessons.html:
Managing the learning environment

  • Prepare a session plan: outcomes, timing, activities, materials, assessment opportunities and a plan B (e.g. rain during a field session).
  • Open well: introductions, expectations, ground rules, and the link to learners' work.
  • Safety: practical sessions with tools, chemicals or animals need briefing, PPE and supervision in line with the OHS Act 85 of 1993.
  • Inclusion: give quieter learners a voice (pairs, small groups), manage dominant participants tactfully, and be sensitive to gender and age dynamics in community groups.
  • Check understanding often with open questions ("What would you do if…?") rather than "Do you understand?".

Handling difficulties

Learners may arrive late because of farm duties, disagree with new practices, or be anxious about written work. Stay calm, acknowledge concerns, link back to evidence and their own experience, and adapt methods: for example, replace a written exercise with an oral report-back or a drawing.

Evaluating the session

Collect feedback from learners (simple smiley-face forms, a round of "one thing I learned, one thing to improve"), observe whether outcomes were achieved, and reflect on your own performance. Record attendance and progress for the training provider or SETA records. Use the evidence to improve the next session.

Key points

  • Facilitation builds on adult learners' experience and focuses on real problems.
  • Use the experiential learning cycle: do, reflect, conceptualise, apply.
  • Match methods to the type of outcome, group and context.
  • Plan sessions with safety, inclusion and a plan B.
  • Evaluate each session and use feedback to improve.
